summary.text: Dubai is the most populous city of the United Arab Emirates, sitting on a creek along the southeastern coast of the Persian Gulf. It grew from a small pearling and fishing settlement into a regional trade hub, and today its economy rests on trade, tourism, aviation, finance and real estate.

facts.label: Origins
facts.value: Founded in the early 18th century as a pearling and fishing settlement; it became a trade hub in the 20th century after declaring itself a free port in 1901.

facts.label: Skyline
facts.value: Home to the Burj Khalifa, the world's tallest building, as part of one of the world's densest skylines.

facts.label: Reclaimed coast
facts.value: Land-reclamation projects have added more than 300 kilometres (190 miles) of artificial coastline.

facts.label: Air hub
facts.value: Dubai International Airport is the world's busiest airport for international passenger traffic, handling over 92 million passengers in 2024.

summary.text: Jerusalem is a city on a plateau in the Judaean Mountains, between the Mediterranean Sea and the Dead Sea. It is one of the oldest cities in the world and is holy to Judaism, Christianity and Islam. Its political status remains disputed and is not widely settled internationally.

facts.label: Holy city
facts.value: Considered a holy city by the three major Abrahamic religions: Judaism, Christianity and Islam.

facts.label: Old City
facts.value: The walled Old City covers only about 0.9 square kilometres and has been divided since the 19th century into the Armenian, Christian, Jewish and Muslim quarters.

facts.label: City walls
facts.value: The present walls were rebuilt in 1538 under the Ottoman sultan Suleiman the Magnificent.

facts.label: World Heritage
facts.value: The Old City became a World Heritage Site in 1981 and is also on the List of World Heritage in Danger.

media.alt: The golden Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem's Old City, seen across the valley from the Mount of Olives.

summary.text: The Dead Sea is a landlocked salt lake in the Jordan Rift Valley, bordered by Jordan, the West Bank and Israel. Its shores are the lowest land-based elevation on Earth, and its extreme salt content makes floating effortless. The lake has long drawn visitors and is steadily shrinking.

facts.label: Elevation
facts.value: As of 2025 the surface is 439.78 metres (1,443 feet) below sea level, the lowest land-based elevation on Earth.

facts.label: Salinity
facts.value: With a salinity of about 34.2% (in 2011), it is roughly 9.6 times as salty as the ocean, and its density makes swimming similar to floating.

facts.label: Depth
facts.value: About 304 metres (997 feet) deep, making it the deepest hypersaline lake in the world.

facts.label: Receding shoreline
facts.value: Its surface area is about 605 square kilometres today, down from 1,050 square kilometres in 1930.

media.alt: A beach on the Jordanian shore of the Dead Sea, with parasols standing near the calm water.
media.attribution: لا روسا, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

summary.text: Persepolis was the ceremonial capital of the Achaemenid Empire, set on the plains of Marvdasht in Iran's Fars province and ringed by the southern Zagros Mountains. Its palaces stood on a raised platform and mark a high point of Achaemenid architecture. It is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

facts.label: Era
facts.value: Ceremonial capital of the Achaemenid Empire (c. 550–330 BC); its earliest remains date back to 515 BC.

facts.label: Fall
facts.value: Taken by the army of Alexander the Great in 330 BC, after which its wooden parts were destroyed by fire.

facts.label: Scholarship
facts.value: Study of the site from the early 17th century led to the modern rediscovery of cuneiform writing, and its trilingual royal inscriptions helped begin the decipherment of cuneiform in the early 19th century.

facts.label: World Heritage
facts.value: Designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1979.

media.alt: The Tachara palace at Persepolis, a stone building with a stairway on the ancient terrace, seen from the southeast.
media.attribution: Laurens R. Krol, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

summary.text: Wadi Rum is a valley cut into sandstone and granite in southern Jordan, close to the Saudi border and about 60 km east of Aqaba. Also called the Valley of the Moon, it is the largest wadi in Jordan, and prehistoric peoples left rock carvings and ruins there.

facts.label: Size
facts.value: Covers about 720 square kilometres, making it the largest wadi (river valley) in Jordan.

facts.label: Location
facts.value: Lies in southern Jordan, about 60 km (37 miles) east of the city of Aqaba.

facts.label: Rock art
facts.value: Khaz'ali Canyon holds petroglyphs of humans and antelopes dating to Thamudic times.

facts.label: World Heritage
facts.value: The Wadi Rum Protected Area has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 2011.

media.alt: A sandstone mountain rising near the entrance to Wadi Rum in Jordan.
media.attribution: Daniel Case, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

summary.text: Karnak is a vast complex of temples, pylons, chapels and other buildings near Luxor in Egypt. Work began in the Middle Kingdom and continued into the Ptolemaic period, though most surviving structures come from the New Kingdom. It was the main place of worship of the Theban Triad, led by the god Amun.

facts.label: Long construction
facts.value: Building began under Senusret I in the Middle Kingdom and continued into the Ptolemaic Kingdom (305–30 BCE).

facts.label: Many builders
facts.value: Approximately thirty pharaohs contributed to the buildings, giving the site a size and diversity not seen elsewhere.

facts.label: Great Hypostyle Hall
facts.value: The hall in the Precinct of Amun-Re covers 5,000 square metres and holds 134 massive columns arranged in 16 rows.

facts.label: World Heritage
facts.value: Added to the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1979 along with the rest of ancient Thebes.

summary.text: Abu Simbel is a site of two massive rock-cut temples in Upper Egypt, on the western bank of Lake Nasser near the Sudanese border. Carved in the 13th century BC during the reign of Ramesses II, the temples are known for the colossal figures of the pharaoh on their facade. In 1968 the whole complex was moved to higher ground to save it from the rising lake.

facts.label: Two temples
facts.value: The Great Temple is dedicated to Ramesses II himself, and the Small Temple to his chief wife, Queen Nefertari.

facts.label: Relocation
facts.value: The complex was relocated in its entirety in 1968 to higher ground to avoid being submerged by Lake Nasser, as part of the International Campaign to Save the Monuments of Nubia.

facts.label: Rediscovery
facts.value: Covered over time by a sand dune, the temples remained unknown to Europeans until March 1813, when the Swiss researcher Johann Ludwig Burckhardt found the small temple and the top frieze of the main temple.

facts.label: Location
facts.value: About 230 km (140 miles) southwest of Aswan, on the western bank of Lake Nasser.

media.alt: Rock-cut temple facade at Abu Simbel in Aswan Governorate, southern Egypt.
